n: In this lecture we shall consider the morphology of shock from the forensic medical point of view. Shock is a severe condition of the body in response to various external influences, characterised above all by a severe disturbance of cardiovascular function. In forensic thanatology, shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, that is DIC syndrome, and the general adaptation syndrome are regarded as general reactions of the body to injury. If a sign of at least one of these reactions is found, it indicates that the injury that provoked it was inflicted during life.

t: The concept and types of shock
n: On the concept and types of shock. Shock develops not only after mechanical injury, that is traumatic and haemorrhagic influence, but also after burns, allergic reaction, sepsis and other causes. The types are: traumatic, haemorrhagic, burn, anaphylactic and septic shock. Pigolkin also lists bacterial-endotoxin, toxic, cardiogenic, hypovolaemic and burn shock. Remember: in all types, more or less identical changes occur in the macrocirculation and especially the microcirculation.

t: Microcirculation in shock: centralisation, sludge and DIC
n: Let us consider the microcirculation in shock: centralisation, sludge and DIC. When the circulation becomes centralised, blood flow in the heart and brain increases, while in the capillaries of the other organs it decreases. Disturbance of capillary circulation leads to altered metabolism and metabolic acidosis. Blood pools in the capillaries and plasma escapes into the interstitial tissue; platelets adhere, while erythrocytes form rouleaux, that is sludge. In shock this process is called disseminated intravascular coagulation, or DIC syndrome.

t: Diagnosis of shock and its difference from blood loss
n: The diagnosis of shock and how it differs from blood loss. In a corpse, the diagnosis of shock rests on a combined assessment of clinical data, the nature of the injury and the pathological changes characteristic of shock. The diagnosis of shock is a clinical diagnosis, so the expert must analyse the case history carefully. The difficulty is that the symptoms of shock and massive blood loss are similar. According to clinicians, the clinical signs of shock in the first hours are associated with a 75 per cent blood loss.

t: Blood loss: acute versus profuse blood loss
n: Now we shall look at the difference between acute and profuse blood loss. In acute blood loss, only the brain and myocardium are anaemic; the spleen is, as usual, full of blood. In profuse blood loss, the skin is dry and pale, and the internal organs, including the spleen, are anaemic and contracted. According to the table, in acute blood loss the volume may be up to 500 ml, death occurs in the first minutes, and cadaveric lividity and rigor mortis are as usual. In profuse blood loss the volume exceeds 50%, that is more than 2.5 l; death occurs over several hours, cadaveric lividity is late and less marked, and rigor mortis is stronger. Attention: these signs are not identical, so do not confuse them.

On the morphology of traumatic shock. Traumatic shock presents with a serious disturbance of the nervous, cardiovascular and endocrine systems. Peripheral circulation is insufficient: the amount of circulating blood does not match the capacity of the vascular system. The diagram shows the chain: injury, nervous, cardiac and endocrine disturbance, circulatory insufficiency, mismatch between blood volume and vascular capacity. Grade III–IV shock usually leads to death; in this case venous congestion and blood depot in the liver and spleen are found.

t: Traumatic shock: clinical features and stages
n: The clinical features and stages of traumatic shock. Shock is an acute disturbance of cardiac and circulatory function, manifested by cold, moist skin, slow blood flow, dyspnoea, oliguria, tachycardia and a fall in pressure. In trauma, shock may be haemorrhagic and painful; painful shock is associated with disturbed nervous regulation. Full development usually takes 5–10 hours after injury. Three stages are distinguished: erethic, that is excitation with relatively high pressure; torpid, in which pressure, especially pulse pressure, falls; and terminal, in which dystrophic and necrotic changes develop.

The criteria for identifying traumatic shock according to Pigolkin are as follows. The first is a characteristic clinical picture and severe injury: damage to large vessels, parenchymatous organs or reflexogenic zones. The second is haemoconcentration and pathological pooling in the capillaries, especially in the spleen and liver. The third is the “shock kidney”: ischaemic cortex and congested pyramids, which results from shunting of blood flow. In addition, microcirculatory disturbance: stromal oedema, sludge, stasis; signs of DIC syndrome are hyaline thrombi and haemorrhages. Finally, parenchymal dystrophy of the organs, foci of necrosis and acute erosions of the gastric mucosa are found.

t: Morphological picture of shock and the endocrine organs
n: The morphological picture of shock and the endocrine organs. Morphologically, shock is characterised by a distinctive redistribution of blood: venous congestion, arteriospasm and spasm of the shunting vessels are observed. The rheological properties of the blood are disturbed, which may progress to DIC syndrome. In any prolonged shock, the general adaptation syndrome, that is alarm, strain and decompensation, produces a morphological equivalent in the endocrine organs.

t: Changes found in a corpse after early death from shock
n: Changes found in a corpse after early death from shock. There is little blood in the cardiac chambers and large vessels, and the blood is fluid. The capillaries of the internal organs are congested. In the “shock kidney” the cortex is anaemic, while the juxtamedullary zone and pyramids are congested; later, dystrophic and necrotic changes appear in the tubules. Sometimes “shock lung” is found: congestive hyperaemia, alveolar oedema, atelectasis, coin-shaped erythrocytes and capillary microthrombi.

t: General definition of shock and morphological signs (Pigolkin)
n: The general definition of shock and its morphological signs according to Pigolkin. Shock is a generalised neurovascular reaction to injury, manifested by centralisation of the circulation, hypotension and sequestration of blood. Its pathogenesis rests on excessively strong nervous afferentation from the zone of injury, redistribution of blood and disturbance of its rheological properties. The signs are: congestion of the microcirculatory vessels, fluid state of the blood, aggregation of erythrocytes, thrombi and haemorrhages. The signs of centralisation are shown by the “shock kidney”, while the secondary changes are dystrophic and necrotic: necrotic nephrosis and necrosis of the liver parenchyma.

t: The three phases of shock and morphological findings
n: The three phases of shock and morphological findings. In the first phase, neuropsychic excitation, transient hypertension and excessive release of catecholamines and glucocorticoids from the adrenal glands are observed. In the second phase pulse pressure falls, stupor appears and the classic clinical and morphological picture of shock develops. In the third phase the haemodynamic changes reach a degree incompatible with life, and coma and dyscirculatory changes in the internal organs are observed. In a corpse, mainly phases II and III are identified morphologically.

t: DIC syndrome: a companion of shock
n: DIC syndrome is regarded as a companion of shock. It often accompanies the development of shock: the rheological properties of the blood are generally disturbed. Thrombi form in the capillaries and venules, and generalised haemorrhages occur owing to damage to the microcirculatory vessels. With thrombus formation the coagulation reserve of the blood decreases. The morphological signs are haemorrhages and various thrombi in the microcirculatory vessels.

t: General adaptation syndrome (Selye) and the age of injury
n: On the general adaptation syndrome, that is Selye's syndrome, and the age of injury. This is the neuroendocrine, that is stress, reaction of the body to any extreme influence. It has three stages: alarm, resistance and decompensation; each has its own morphological picture. This picture helps to determine the duration, that is the age, of the injury. In the first phase the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenocortical system is activated and the capillary endothelium swells.

On burn shock. The first period of burn disease is burn shock, which is based on a systemic disturbance of the microcirculation. Excessive pain impulses from the focus also contribute to the development of shock; the shock itself usually does not exceed 2–3 days. In those who die during the period of shock, hypovolaemia, pathological blood depot, disturbance of microcirculation and rheology, and hypoxic changes are found. According to Iskandarov, burn shock usually lasts up to 1 day, sometimes 2–3 days.

t: Features of burn shock from the expert's point of view
n: Let us consider the features of burn shock from the expert's point of view. Unlike traumatic shock, burn shock runs with a prolonged erethic period of up to 3 days: normal or high pressure, reduced blood volume and prolonged pain are observed. Old age is regarded as a factor that increases the risk of death at the same severity of burn. The morphological picture differs in a considerably more marked congestion of the internal organs than in other types of shock. In burn shock, interneuronal connections in the sensorimotor cortex of the brain change, that is, morphological changes occur in the synapses.

The haemodynamic mechanism of electric shock. Electric shock, like other shocks, is associated with a mismatch between the energy consumption and energy supply of the tissues. When the circulation is centralised, blood accumulates mainly in the central vital organs; this is the compensation stage, that is grade I shock. In the deep torpid phase, peripheral vascular tone falls and blood is deposited at the periphery, which is called “blood loss into one's own vessels”. If vascular tone is lost completely, the blood cannot fill the entire vascular system, and reversible and irreversible decompensation develops, that is grades III and IV.

The pathomorphological signs of electric shock. First, haemoconcentration and DIC syndrome occur together with haemorrhagic syndrome. Vascular permeability changes, and sequestration of blood and shunting of blood flow are observed in the microcirculatory vessels. Various dystrophic processes occur in nervous tissue, and glycogen is rapidly mobilised from the tissue depots. Owing to disturbance of metabolism and of renal excretory function, acetonaemia and azotaemia appear, and the organs suffer circulatory-hypoxic damage.

To conclude. Shock is a generalised reaction running with centralisation of the circulation, hypotension and sequestration of blood; microcirculatory changes are common to all types. In early death there is little blood in the heart and large vessels, and it is fluid, while the capillaries of the internal organs are congested; “shock kidney” and sometimes “shock lung” are found. The symptoms of shock and massive blood loss are similar, and the diagnosis of shock is a clinical diagnosis. Burn and electric shock have distinctive features: a prolonged erethic period and marked congestion, as well as glycogen mobilisation and acetonaemia.
